research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-14, first run, mode create, empty baseline, no prior evidence or research notes). Logged 41 sources: 39 opened, 2 not opened (S33 Telegraph, HTTP 402 paywall; S34 Music Week On The Radar, paywalled after the first sentence). Read in full: Rolling Stone UK, SSENSE, Interview, Notion, NYLON, Vogue, Atwood, Principle, Euphoria and two Music Week pieces (S01-S11), plus caption transcripts of 15 video interviews dated November 2025 to October 2026, about 45,000 words (S13-S25, S36, S37, S41). Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen. Outcome: no defensible discriminator; subject meets open-case eligibility (adult, 21; breakthrough October 2025; entire first-person record is two promotional cycles). Status ready, profile_format open_case, leading read Type 4 at low confidence, Type 2 the strongest alternative, Type 3 live; Types 6 and 9 tested and set aside. Risks set: contested_typing (required for open cases) and sensitive_allegations (C24 her account of a relationship at 19 with an unnamed older man; C03 an unnamed producer's 'false promises'; C29 critics' nepotism and industry-plant framing; also extensive health disclosures, C26, C27), so the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-14). Latest developments found: MTV VMA Best New Artist on September 27, 2026 (S29); 'Great Expectation' at No. 1 in the UK in September 2026 (S29); Austin City Limits set on October 9, 2026, reviewed under a 'nepo baby' headline (S28); Austin City Limits TV episode on October 3-4, 2026 (S25); My House tour began October 13, 2026 at the Ryman, North American leg to November 10, 2026 (S38). Grammy nominations are due November 16, 2026 (S39). No statement from her on the nepotism framing was found. open_case.next_review is 2026-12-01, after the nominations and the end of the North American leg.

Drafting guidance (open case). Follow the standard's 'Open case profiles' section. Open with who she is and why people are searching (the VMA win, 'Die on This Hill', a UK No. 1, a sold-out world tour), then name the open question: is the person who says she is 'naturally sad' and has always felt like a 'visitor' a Four, or is the more revealing line her own 'I had to make myself needed'? Show what the record shows, dated and sourced, with limits. Set Type 4 beside Types 2 and 3 with the best evidence for and against each. Include an H2 beginning '## What would settle it' built from open_case.settle_signals. Keep '## What is Sienna Spiro's personality type?' with an answer of at most 60 words in 'leading read, held loosely' language. Target 1,200 to 2,500 words. Titles, description and FAQs must say 'leading read' or 'open case', never 'is a Type 4'. Set enneagram: 4 and published: false.

Strongest material for the draft (all verified in sources): the assembly song at 10 sung to the children who bullied her (S04, S05, S37); the ELAM wait-list and daily emails (S01, S10); 'I had to make myself needed ... the biggest theme throughout my whole life' (S18); imagining the man who never came standing outside her New York apartment each morning (S13, S16); the applause moment that became 'Pure' (S13, S15); the suit she wore to the studio when she felt unaccomplished (S13); the full-take method that began as laziness (S13, S14); the conflicting 'Die on This Hill' accounts (S02, S05, S06, S13, S20).

Sensitivity. (a) The older man (C24): her account only; he is unnamed; describe it in her words and dates, do not speculate about identity or call it abuse or a crime, and do not use it to diagnose her. (b) The producer whose promise led her to leave school (C03): unnamed; her words only. (c) Health (C26): report ADHD, nodules, body image and eating difficulty, and depression only as she disclosed them, with no diagnosis-led personality claims; do not attribute OCD to her (the AP interviewer said it about herself). (d) Her mother's illness (C27): concerns another person; one clause at most, framed as she framed it, no update. (e) Nepotism (C29): state her father's profession plainly, attribute the 'nepo baby' and 'industry plant' labels to the outlets that used them, note that no reporting shows money bought her career, and do not use the labels in the article's own voice or as evidence of motive.

Quotation cautions. S13-S25, S36, S37 and S41 are YouTube auto-caption transcripts without speaker labels; check every printed quotation against the audio and its timestamp, and remove only clear stutters. Do not quote as hers: the 'Capricorn'/'Libra' exchange or 'good 70%er' in S16; the host's 'baby sibling syndrome' remarks in S18; 'ADHD and OCD' in S14. In S22 the captions render 'Back to Blonde' as 'Back to Black'. The Vevo DSCVR, Rolling Stone (nodules) and Telegraph quotations exist only secondhand via Hey Alma (S26); attribute them as reported or verify the originals. Euphoria's introduction wrongly claims a Hot 100 Top 10 (her peak is No. 19). SSENSE's page metadata date (2025-08-12) is wrong; use November 12, 2025. Notion calls her 'nineteen' in a piece published when she was 20. NYLON's 'innate sadness' is the writer's paraphrase with a two-word quotation. Sung lyrics in S25 captions are unreliable; use the official lyric sheet.

Follow-up worth doing before or at the next refresh: (1) open the Telegraph interview (May 20, 2026) and the Music Week On The Radar profile (January 20, 2026) through subscriptions; (2) find and transcribe the Vevo DSCVR interview and the original Rolling Stone nodules interview, the ELLE interview of April 2026 about a breakup, Elton John's Rocket Hour conversation and the 15 Questions interview; (3) look for any long-form interview given after October 13, 2026 on the tour; (4) look for testimony from Omer Fedi, Sam Smith, Edie Rose, her sisters or ELAM contemporaries; (5) check whether she has responded anywhere to the nepotism framing.

Draft log (2026-10-14, mode create, empty baseline). Wrote draft.md as an open case: leading read Type 4 at low confidence, Type 2 the closest rival, Type 3 live, Types 6 and 9 set aside. Mapped the claims below to exact passages in the body or frontmatter. No new source was added; excerpts and locators of already-opened sources were extended to cover what the draft prints. Every quotation in the body and FAQs was matched by script against the saved source texts and caption transcripts in /tmp/sienna-spiro-research (scratch files that may not survive). Quotations drop clear spoken repeats ('would would', 'it's it's', 'I just I just', 'I'll I'll'); each affected source's locator says so.

Audio second transcription at draft stage (Whisper small.en on segments cut from yt-dlp downloads; a machine transcription, not a human listen): S13, S14, S15, S16, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23 and S24 at the timestamps named in each locator. Every printed quotation from those segments matched. Where captions and Whisper differ by a word ('so so empty'/'so empty', 'gonna'/'going to clap', 'a suit the studio'/'a suit to the studio'), the draft paraphrases or prints only the shared words. NOT second-transcribed, so a verifier should re-listen: S18 at about 11:20 ('because it's actually exhausting', C53); S24 'my least favorite emotion' (C39); S17 'was very depressed at the time' and 'very superstitious' (C62, C33); S36 sister lyric (C46); S41 'knowing you're temporary to someone' (C08). The grandmother line (C31, S21) has no speaker label; it follows the host's question to 'Grandma Sheila' in both transcriptions.

Claims removed from the draft inventory because the draft does not print them: C19 (control freak / 'people gravitate towards authenticity'), C25 (art as received, no-windows studio), C27 (her mother's illness, left out on sensitivity grounds), C30 (Variety's 'modesty' line), C32 ('terrible talker', least masking on stage) and C34 ('technically a terrible singer', songs mostly bad). Their sources are retained. Hypothesis text revised accordingly: references to C15's 'perceive me' quotation, C19 and C34 and the 'feel really secure' uniform detail were removed from alternative_case; leading type, rival, confidence, discriminator and settle signals are unchanged. for_claim_ids now lists only retained claims.

Research-stage material deliberately not printed: the explicit age gap with the older man (she is quoted only as calling it 'not healthy' and saying he 'did not have good intentions with me'); the unnamed producer beyond her own sentence; her mother's illness; OCD (the AP interviewer's, not hers); streaming totals. The Vevo DSCVR quotations (C14, C38) are attributed as quoted by Hey Alma because the original video was not opened.

Length note for the editor: checkDraft counts about 2,750 words, above the open-case target of roughly 1,200 to 2,500 (well inside the 4,500 ceiling). First cuts if the jury wants it shorter: the AP full-take paragraph (C20), the 'Die on This Hill' tellings paragraph (C16, C58), the team-credit paragraph (C23) and the Variety Adele sentence (C36). Budget any additions against cuts; edit stages on this pipeline have tended to add length.

Edit log (2026-10-14, edit stage). Six-role jury adjudicated (38 findings). Four reviewers (fan-01, critic-01, enneagram-01, future-02) showed from the transcripts that the draft's reason for leading with Four inverted its sources: the closed-off withdrawal is a past phase she rejects (S13 ~04:30, S14 ~14:50, S16 ~18:00), 'if you don't want me, don't have me' is acceptance of endings followed by 'very loyal ... valuable to some people' (S19 ~14:10-14:40), and the giving is present tense (S13 ~49:00; S21 ~07:00). The editor re-weighed the case without the tense test: the Two evidence is explicit, repeated in five interviews from November 2025 to June 2026 and still present tense, while the Four evidence (longing, unreality, sadness as temperament) is the kind the article itself discounts as genre currency and carries depression/ADHD confounds. The leading read therefore moves from Type 4 to Type 2, held loosely at low confidence; Four becomes the closest rival and Three stays live. This is a type-thesis change after the frozen review, so risks.major_thesis_change is set and the run must hold for scripts/run-blog-pipeline.sh Sienna-Spiro --refresh --expanded-review; the edit does not absorb the change.

Edit stage, verification notes: these printed quotations are caption-only and were not second-transcribed; a verifier should re-listen: S21 visitor definition 'you're expired to them' (~06:50-07:10); S19 'I'm a very loyal and I can be very valuable to some people' (~14:30); S41 continuation 'and knowing you probably care about that person more than they care about you' (~02:20); S18 'because it's actually exhausting' (~11:20); S14 'quite an over-thinker' (~02:00) and 'a control freak' (~15:40); S16 'I've had that so many different times' (~21:00); S13 'I'm actually so stupid sometimes' (~27:20); S17 'very depressed' and the guilt clause (~06:00-06:40). sources.title: Sienna Spiro: 'I'm the most unclassy person ever' (Rolling Stone UK Future of Music cover)
sources.speaker: Sienna Spiro, interviewed by Hannah Ewens (Rolling Stone UK)
sources.locator: Feature body: comparisons paragraph; 'Any love song I write' paragraph; ADHD/'The Visitor' paragraph; ELAM waiting-list anecdote; pandemic and food paragraph; manager Miriam Maslin paragraph; 'My hair felt like armour' paragraph; 'too aware' paragraph near the end. Edit stage (2026-10-14): the ADHD/'The Visitor' quotation, the ELAM anecdote and the 'armour' line were rechecked against the saved page text. The phrase 'honestly quite validating' in the feature attaches to learning how her brain works, so the edit does not print it. 'She hated the idea of being looked at' paraphrases her 'I hated the idea of people being able to see me and perceive me', which she gives as the reason for the baggy clothes she wore early on.
sources.excerpt: "Any love song I write, I've got to flip it – it's always got to have some sadness to it." [...] "That's what a lot of the music is about, like 'The Visitor' – struggling to keep up with people and being [too] aware of everything, you end up losing people – and you're temporary." [...] "I was so sure I was going to get in, I told everyone I did" [...] "I was sending them videos every day." [...] "I hated the idea of people being able to see me and perceive me." [...] "My hair felt like armour. It made me feel more myself, even though it looked less like me," [...] "artists are nothing without their teams," [...] "It's something you have to be really conscious about: making sure everything is coming from you."
sources.context: Cover feature from the June/July 2026 issue: a London shoot plus a later phone interview from Stockholm, during the run-up to the debut album. The writer supplies the context that she 'slipped between friend groups', the ADHD framing ('masking to fit in', 'out of sight, out of mind') and the description of a 'lifelong issue with food and eating' that got 'really bad' in the pandemic; those are partly paraphrase, not her words. Source for her crediting manager Miriam Maslin, met at 16.

sources.title: Sienna Spiro Is Wise Beyond Her Years (SSENSE)
sources.speaker: Sienna Spiro, interviewed over Zoom by Iana Murray (SSENSE)
sources.locator: Q&A section: answers to 'Heartbreak feels like the throughline', 'TikTok has played such a major role', 'You played your first live shows this year' and 'In what ways did you have to learn how to be a performer?'
sources.excerpt: "nobody really wanted to be around me when I was younger. I don't know for what reason that was, but I really struggled to keep friends, and my way of dealing with that was overcompensating and giving a lot of myself to people." [...] "I have in the past." [...] "I'm not a natural performer" [...] "I'm very stubborn. And I think when you stick to your vision and be a little bit stubborn, it's so worth it in the end." [...] "I'm a terrible talker. I write songs because I can't talk."
sources.context: Opened via the r.jina.ai reader because the page is script-rendered. The page footer dates the piece November 12, 2025; the page metadata says 2025-08-12, but she answers a question about having 'turned 20', which happened on 2025-09-28, so the November date is used. 'I have in the past' answers whether she has fallen into writing for TikTok's short-form trap. Interview given at home in London after her first UK/EU headline tour.

sources.title: Introducing Sienna Spiro, the Sad Girl Singer Bringing the Sixties Back (Interview Magazine)
sources.speaker: Sienna Spiro, interviewed by Ary Russell (Interview Magazine)
sources.locator: Q&A dated 'TUESDAY 6:13 PM MARCH 17, 2026 LOWER EAST SIDE' (dressing-room conversation): early-career answers, the drop-out exchange, the Omer Fedi/over-singing answer, the TikTok answer about 'The Visitor', the 'nine times' answer and the closing survey joke. Also the answer to "Do you see yourself writing happy songs in the future?" Edit stage: also the 'I ended up finding my management' answer, the 'dropping out for quite a foolish reason' answer and the 'You Stole the Show' answer (reliving songs on stage).
sources.excerpt: "I was a very emotional child. I'm very overwhelmed by things." [...] "I went behind everyone's back. I found a music college, applied to it, kind of didn't get in." [...] "I'm very stubborn and headstrong. When I want to do something, I would just try everything in my power to do it." [...] "It was like false promises, older producer man." [...] "I was trying to prove myself because I actually didn't think I was a good singer growing up. So every chance I would get to over sing, I would do it." [...] "As cool as that is, it will never dictate what I do." [...] "I believed in it so much and everyone was sick of me." [...] "I hope they like me." [...] "I would love to make some upbeat songs." [...] "I ended up finding my management from posting one video." [...] "I was dropping out for quite a foolish reason that, looking back, probably wasn't the right thing to do." [...] "That's what 'You Stole the Show' is about. It's about living it every night and just imagining what would happen if that person was there."
sources.context: Opened via r.jina.ai (interviewmagazine.com blocks direct fetches). Recorded backstage on her first US headline tour. The interviewer's own questions are omitted from the page in places, so some answers lack their prompt. 'False promises, older producer man' is her answer about why she left music college at 16; the producer is not named anywhere in the record.

sources.title: Sienna Spiro And The Art Of Intention (NYLON)
sources.speaker: Sienna Spiro, interviewed over Zoom by Jillian Giandurco (NYLON)
sources.locator: Feature body: 'Die on This Hill' versions paragraph ('Someone around me was like'); 'My dad was my biggest critic' paragraph; 'Lady in the Mirror'/bullying paragraph; songwriting 'speed-dating' paragraph; Omer Fedi/'prove myself' paragraph; 'If I hyperfixate too much on numbers' paragraph; closing 'See, I told you!' line. Edit stage: the assembly paragraph ('look behind to see the mum'), the 'Die on This Hill' TikTok-bridge paragraph and the closing 'once-biggest critic: her dad' paragraph.
sources.excerpt: "Someone around me was like, 'This is it.' And I remember singing it…" [...] "My dad was my biggest critic for the longest time," [...] "I really grew up thinking I wasn't a singer." [...] "I was getting bullied, and no one really believed me that it was happening," [...] "The song was about how the only person who really knows what's going on is me, the person in the mirror." [...] "I really was trying to prove myself," [...] "If I hyperfixate too much on numbers and people liking me, I would be miserable," [...] "I'm like, 'See, I told you!'" [...] "It was just something I always did." [...] "My mum was there filming, and everyone was looking behind. That was so validating." [...] "I always tell him," she says, laughing. (Writer: the first song was "Lady in the Mirror", written at 10; she performed it at a school assembly in front of the children who had bullied her.) [...] "anytime someone was singing on stage, everyone would look behind to see the mum. That was kind of a sign that you're killing it," [...] TikTok quickly grabbed hold of the song's melodramatic bridge [...] It's even better than making a fan out of her once-biggest critic: her dad.
sources.context: Zoom interview from her London bedroom four days after a tour ended, ahead of the album. The writer, not Spiro, supplies 'stubborn, passionate, and bestowed with an "innate sadness" from the age of 10' as a paraphrase with one quoted phrase. Her account here of the 'Die on This Hill' arrangement (someone else thought the guitar version was right; she knew it was not) differs from her later Vogue and Zach Sang accounts (S06, S13). The 'person in the mirror' explanation and the 'sign that you're killing it' explanation are her words in the same paragraph as the assembly story. The writer says she 'chuckles at the memory now' of her father's criticism and closes with her father now a fan.

sources.title: The Timeless Talent of Sienna Spiro (Vogue)
sources.speaker: Sienna Spiro, interviewed in person by Rob LeDonne (Vogue)
sources.locator: Q&A: answers on how 'Die on This Hill' came to be, 'innate sadness', dropping out of ELAM, vintage shopping, and being secure on stage. Edit stage: the 'innate sadness' answer continues directly into 'and I don't think it's a bad thing. I think it's a very normal, human way to be.'
sources.excerpt: "I am very stubborn, as you can probably tell by listening to the song. So I said, "No, it's not."" [...] "he was correct, because it definitely felt right as a ballad." [...] "I was a bit selfish in the way I made music" [...] "I don't mean this to sound sad or make me sound like a victim or anything, but I just think some people are naturally sad, and I definitely feel that way about myself. I think it runs in my family." [...] "My friends would be like, "You're being so dramatic, you're being too much, you're overwhelming us." But I was just being how I was naturally." [...] "When I tried out their styles, it made me feel so myself and confident because I'm a very insecure person." [...] "I really struggled with my mental health growing up." [...] "My dad's this way, my grandma's this way, and I don't think it's a bad thing. I think it's a very normal, human way to be. Some people just wake up and they naturally feel quite low, and they are also absolutely able to experience happy moments."
sources.context: Conducted in the Ludlow Hotel lobby in New York on release day of the debut album; condensed and edited by Vogue. In this account the producer Omer Fedi wanted a ballad, she insisted on an uptempo version, and he was right.

claims.passage: At 10, Sienna Spiro wrote her first song. "Lady in the Mirror" was about being bullied at school when, as she told [NYLON](https://www.nylon.com/entertainment/sienna-spiro-interview-visitor-debut-album-die-on-this-hill-tiktok-new-tour) in June 2026, "no one really believed me that it was happening." "The song was about how the only person who really knows what's going on is me, the person in the mirror." Then she sang it at a school assembly, in front of the children who had bullied her.
claims.inference: The assembly story is told consistently in five interviews from March 2025 to June 2026. Choosing to answer bullies by performing her own song about being misunderstood is an early, costly choice; it fits both a need to be seen as she is (Four) and a need to be validated (NYLON: everyone turning to look at her mother filming 'was so validating').
claims.alternative: All accounts are hers; no classmate or teacher has spoken. Weight-based bullying is a sufficient circumstantial cause of feeling unwanted. Do not write a causal childhood-wound thesis.

claims.inference: The same memory carries a second note, approval from the room. Set beside C69 it shows both being understood and being seen to do well.
claims.alternative: A child enjoying applause implies no type.

claims.passage: > "I don't mean this to sound sad or make me sound like a victim or anything, but I just think some people are naturally sad, and I definitely feel that way about myself. I think it runs in my family."
claims.inference: Repeated in at least four 2026 interviews in nearly identical words, and paraphrased by NYLON as an 'innate sadness' from age 10. It is the self-image she leads with, not a mood she reports passing through, which is the closest the record comes to the Four pattern of identifying with melancholy.

Her genre and manager's strategy reward this self-presentation (C28). She prefaces it with a disclaimer, so she is managing how it lands.

claims.inference: The definition pairs impermanence with unequal care, which fits the Two reading (giving more than she gets) as well as the Four reading (longing for what is not returned).
claims.alternative: A song description in a promotional segment; the continuation is caption-only.

claims.claim: Setting: living in New York in 2025 while opening shows for Sam Smith, involved with an older man who promised he would come.
claims.passage: In 2025, at 19, she was living in New York for a stretch while opening shows for Sam Smith, and she was involved with an older man who, she told Zach Sang, "promised me he would come."
claims.inference: Her account; Wikipedia lists her as a support act on Sam Smith's To Be Free: New York City run in 2025.

claims.claim: She told Zach Sang that in 2025 she imagined the man standing outside her New York apartment every day and wrote pages while waiting for him to come; he never came.
claims.passage: Every day, she said, she walked down the stairs and imagined him outside the door, playing out "what I thought would happen if he was there." She filled pages in a café, "waiting for this guy to come who never came," then went to a jazz club and cried.
claims.inference: Idealizing the absent and longing for what is missing, then turning it into a song, is the most distinctive Four-like pattern in the record.
claims.alternative: Romantic fixation at 17 to 19 is developmentally ordinary; ADHD hyperfocus is her own explanation (S14, S16). Twos also pursue unavailable partners, though usually by giving rather than by fantasy.

claims.inference: A sensitive personal account she chose to make public and to set to music. Relevant only for what she says she was seeking ('I never did get chosen', a 'craving to ... be held') and how she processes loss through songs.
claims.alternative: Her account only; the man is unnamed and no one else has spoken. Do not speculate about his identity, do not present it as an allegation of a crime, and do not use it as evidence of character beyond her own interpretation.

claims.claim: Interpretation: she handles absence by imagining the person present and making a song of it.
claims.passage: What it shows is how she handles absence: she imagines the person into the doorway, then makes a song of it.
claims.inference: Built from C21, C44 and C45.
claims.alternative: Romantic fixation at 19 is developmentally ordinary; ADHD hyperfocus is her own explanation (S14, S16).

claims.claim: "You Stole the Show" (released July 2025) is, she told Interview in March 2026, about reliving a song every night and imagining what would happen if that person were there.
claims.passage: "You Stole the Show," from 2025, is "about living it every night and just imagining what would happen if that person was there," she told [Interview](https://www.interviewmagazine.com/music/introducing-sienna-spiro-the-sad-girl-singer-bringing-the-sixties-back) in March 2026;
claims.inference: A second, earlier instance of imagining an absent person present, about a different relationship from the New York man, so the longing pattern rests on repetition.
claims.alternative: Performing a song nightly invites re-imagining its scene; the habit may be craft as much as temperament.

claims.claim: On Genius, about a near-reunion with the ex in "You Stole the Show", she said she is kind of jealous of her own imagination.
claims.passage: of that ex, she said on Genius, "I'm kind of jealous of my own imagination."
claims.inference: Envy of an imagined scene, explaining "You Stole the Show".
claims.alternative: Lyric commentary in a promotional video.

claims.claim: She told Lyrical Lemonade in August 2026 that, having been let down a lot, she pretends things are real as a protection, and that it has happened many times.
claims.passage: "I think I've been let down a lot by people, and so as like a protective thing, I just pretend something's real when it's not," she told [Lyrical Lemonade](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-vUlYGknBAE) in August 2026. "I've had that so many different times."
claims.inference: Fantasy as protection against disappointment.
claims.alternative: The printed quotation drops a repeated "I just".

claims.passage: "Pure," the song she calls her most personal, came from the reverse, an audience that was there and silent. Performing in 2025, she said on the Zach Sang Show, she caught herself waiting to see whether anyone would clap. Nobody did, and she decided the waiting was "other people's agenda being pushed into mine."
claims.inference: She rejected applause-seeking as foreign to her, but on a night the applause was withheld; the episode is ambiguous between principle and face-saving.
claims.alternative: Reframing a disappointment after withheld approval fits Two or Three as well as Four.

claims.claim: She says she wrote "Pure" while very depressed and guilty about working in Los Angeles while her mother was ill in London.
claims.passage: She wrote the song while "very depressed," she told [iHeartRadio](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1eJ8qdFBVI), and guilty about working in Los Angeles while her mother was ill in London.
claims.inference: Her own account of the song's circumstances; it includes guilt toward her mother as well as depression, which keeps the song from being read as Four-only material.

claims.passage: Of one line, "I wish I was real," she told [Billboard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FknTvkR0FmY) on October 2, 2026, "I'm a really existential person and sometimes I just don't feel like a real person."
claims.inference: Feeling unreal fits the Four search for a real self.
claims.alternative: She ties it in the same answer to feeling depressed; written during the depression she describes (C62).

claims.claim: Context of the Z100 answer: asked why she felt like a visitor; she cited growing up bigger than her friends.
claims.passage: In March 2026 she told [Z100](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ybJbtoygyaE), the New York pop station, that she grew up bigger than her friends, and people weren't very nice, "especially when you're young."
claims.inference: The prompt and her stated cause.
claims.alternative: Weight-based unkindness is a sufficient circumstantial cause of feeling unwanted.

claims.claim: In March 2026 she told Z100 that because she was never really wanted around she had to make herself needed and of service to people.
claims.passage: > "I always felt like I was never really wanted around. So, I had to make myself like needed. So, I would always try and like, you know, make myself of service to people."
claims.inference: This is a direct, specific, unprompted first-person description of the Two strategy (earning a place by being needed and helpful), given four times across five months. It is the strongest single piece of evidence against the leading read.
claims.alternative: She narrates it as the past ('I've been like that for ages') and as the source of the visitor feeling, then says she learned to stop because it was 'exhausting'. A Four under strain can over-give to secure relationships; that arrow explanation must not be used to dismiss it. A bullied child making herself useful is also a common adaptation that implies no type.

claims.claim: She called the therapist role the biggest theme of her life.
claims.passage: > "I've kind of been that like therapist role for my friends where I've always taken on so much of people's problems because I never thought people would want me otherwise if they didn't need me. So that's genuinely been like the biggest theme throughout my whole life."
claims.inference: The single strongest first-person statement for the Two alternative.
claims.alternative: The printed quotation drops a repeated "would". The host follows with his own therapy remark, which is not hers.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Z100 answer is a plain description of the Two strategy and recurs.
claims.passage: That is about as plain a description of the Type 2 strategy as anyone gives in an interview, and it wasn't a one-off.
claims.inference: Supported by C48 to C51.
claims.alternative: A bullied child making herself useful is a common adaptation that implies no type.

claims.claim: She told SSENSE that she dealt with struggling to keep friends by overcompensating and giving a lot of herself.
claims.passage: She told [SSENSE](https://www.ssense.com/en-gb/editorial/music/sienna-spiro-is-wise-beyond-her-years) in November 2025 that she struggled to keep friends as a child, and "my way of dealing with that was overcompensating and giving a lot of myself to people."
claims.inference: Same strategy, told four months earlier.
claims.alternative: Past tense; about childhood.

claims.claim: Explaining "Die on This Hill" for Genius in February 2026, she said she sometimes mirrors the people around her to be kept around.
claims.passage: On Genius in February 2026 she said, "I sometimes mirror the people around me to be kept around."
claims.inference: Shame (embarrassment), pride as a defence, and mirroring to be kept around place her motivation in the heart/image triad (Two, Three or Four) rather than elsewhere. Mirroring to be kept is closest to Two or Three; it is evidence against an independent, unaffected Four.
claims.alternative: 'Pride' is used in its everyday sense, not as Enneagram vocabulary; the commentary is a promotional video recorded as the song peaked.

claims.claim: In April 2026 she defined being a visitor, on Capital, as knowing you are temporary to somebody and expired to them if you do not show up in a specific way.
claims.passage: And in April 2026 she gave [Capital](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2o4ftjqGfUM) her definition of the album's title word: "It's knowing you're temporary to somebody and knowing if you don't show up in that specific way, you're expired to them."
claims.inference: Her own definition of the album concept is conditional belonging: kept while she keeps showing up. That is the Two's bargain stated in the present tense, after her breakthrough.
claims.alternative: Caption-only and not second-transcribed; it is a song explanation in a radio segment and could describe a shared adolescent experience rather than a motive.

claims.claim: She told Zach Sang in June 2026 that she always feels she gives a lot of herself, will do anything for someone she loves, and has been taken advantage of.
claims.passage: She tells the giving in the present tense, too. "I always feel like I give a lot of myself," she told Zach Sang in June 2026. "So if I love somebody I'll do anything." It has, she added, "been taken advantage of a bit in my life."
claims.inference: Present-tense, post-breakthrough giving with the Two's typical complaint of being taken advantage of; it refutes the draft's claim that the helper is only her past.
claims.alternative: Generosity toward loved ones and feeling used are common; the statement alone does not show that being needed is the motive.

claims.claim: She told Z100 in March 2026 that, afraid of losing people, she held on so tightly that they left, and had to learn not to because it was exhausting.
claims.passage: Afraid of losing people, she held on so tightly that they left, she told Z100, and had to learn not to, "because it's actually exhausting."
claims.inference: What she says she changed is clinging, not helping.
claims.alternative: Clinging fits Two, Four or Six; caption-only, not second-transcribed.

claims.claim: She told Zach Sang she went through a phase of being completely opposed to relationships because they would end, which left her very closed off and very sad.
claims.passage: Then came a phase of shutting down: she was "completely opposed to being in a relationship" because it would end, she told Zach Sang, until "I became very closed off and I became very sad."
claims.inference: The withdrawal is told in the past tense and rejected ("it's really not the way to live"); AP and Lyrical Lemonade tell it the same way. It is not her present stance.
claims.alternative: A closed-off phase after hurt fits a Four's withdrawal or a Two's defensive retreat.

claims.claim: She says the album is about getting out of the closed-off phase; its closing song is named for mono no aware, which she glossed for the AP in July 2026 as the gentle sadness of knowing everything beautiful is temporary and loving it more because it will not last.
claims.passage: The album, as she tells it, is about getting out of that phase. Its closing song is named for the Japanese phrase _mono no aware_, "the gentle sadness of knowing everything beautiful is temporary and loving it more because it won't last," as she glossed it for the [Associated Press](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WFpFT3u6seI) in July 2026.
claims.inference: The album's stated arc runs from fear of endings and closing off to accepting them; she says the same to Zach Sang (June 2026) and from the Austin City Limits stage ("this whole album is about this like massive fear of impermanence I had").
claims.alternative: The arc is self-narrated inside the campaign for the album that dramatizes it.

claims.claim: On July 8, 2026, she told Z100 her new stance on endings: so be it, allow it to end, if you don't want me, don't have me.
claims.passage: On July 8, 2026, she put the new stance to [Z100](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aJRofzOtKmg): "So be it. Allow it to end. Like if you don't want me, don't have me."
claims.inference: In context the line rejects her old refusal to enter relationships that might end; it is acceptance, not withdrawal.
claims.alternative: It can also be read as self-protection; she follows it with a case for her own value.

claims.claim: She followed it by saying she is very loyal and can be very valuable to some people.
claims.passage: A moment later: "I'm a very loyal and I can be very valuable to some people."
claims.inference: Even her acceptance of endings is framed through her value to others, which fits the Two reading.
claims.alternative: Caption-only (Whisper segment ends earlier); a self-affirmation in a fan-facing segment.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the change she describes runs from clinging to closing off to letting things end; she never describes dropping the helping.
claims.passage: So the change she describes runs from clinging, to closing off, to letting things end. The helping is the one part she never describes dropping.
claims.inference: Across Z100 (March 2026), Capital (April), Zach Sang (June), AP (July), Z100 (July) and Lyrical Lemonade (August), what she says she changed is clinging and closing off; the helper role is told in present perfect ("I've been like that for ages") and present tense.
claims.alternative: She might have said elsewhere, in unread sources, that she stopped people-pleasing; none of the opened sources says so.

claims.claim: She applied only to ELAM, told everyone she had got in, was wait-listed, and sent the school videos every day until it let her in.
claims.passage: As a teenager she applied to one school, East London Arts & Music, and was so sure of a place that "I told everyone I did," she told [Rolling Stone UK](https://www.rollingstone.co.uk/music/sienna-spiro-future-of-music-cover-interview-visitor-61532/) in May 2026. She was wait-listed. "I was sending them videos every day," she said, and eventually the school let her in.
claims.inference: Told consistently in four interviews from March 2025 to July 2026. The ELAM petition is a concrete, costly-in-face episode of single-minded persistence; the drop-out reason she gives (false promises from an unnamed older producer) is a hinge in her story that she declines to elaborate ('I won't get into it now', Vogue).
claims.alternative: Ordinary teenage impulsiveness and an industry that courts teenagers explain the drop-out without a personality account; she had already been signed by a manager (Vogue). The producer is unnamed; treat it as her account, make no allegation about any identifiable person.

claims.claim: She left school at 16 on a big producer's promise and later called it quite a foolish reason.
claims.passage: She left at 16 because, she told [Principle](https://principlemagazine.com/2025/03/10/sienna-spiro/) in March 2025, "I was promised by this big producer that something would happen." She has not named him, and a year later she told Interview it was "quite a foolish reason."
claims.inference: An impulsive, costly choice on a promise.
claims.alternative: The producer is unnamed; her account only. The "16" comes from the interviewer's question, which she did not dispute.

claims.claim: She describes her pace as "next thing, next thing, next thing".
claims.passage: Her pace, in the Principle interview: "I'm like, 'Oh, next thing, next thing, next thing.'"
claims.inference: Forward drive; it fits the Three alternative.
claims.alternative: Said about not pausing to reflect on the EP's reception, which she then did.

claims.claim: Her father was her biggest critic for a long time; she laughs about it now that he is a fan.
claims.passage: Her father was "my biggest critic for the longest time," she told NYLON, laughing about it now that he is a fan.
claims.inference: Approval-seeking through performance is acknowledged in four 2026 interviews, with a clear source (a critical father) and a clear correction (Fedi). Wanting to prove her father wrong ('See, I told you!') is a recurring note.
claims.alternative: Reads as Three (performing for recognition) and as Two (seeking approval); a Four reading would say it was compensation for a deficient sense of self. Young singers commonly over-sing; the correction came from a producer, so it is not purely her own choice.

claims.claim: She told Zach Sang she loved the validation and over-sang for compliments.
claims.passage: > "And I really loved that validation. And so I would do the most. I would do every riff, every run."
claims.inference: Approval-seeking through performance, early in her career.
claims.alternative: Young singers commonly over-sing; she frames it as corrected by Omer Fedi.

claims.claim: On a day she was not feeling accomplished she wore a suit to the studio, and called herself "so stupid sometimes", laughing.
claims.passage: And on a day she wasn't "feeling accomplished," she told Zach Sang, her "solution to that was wearing a suit" to the studio. "I'm actually so stupid sometimes," she added, laughing.
claims.inference: A self-mocking story about dressing to feel accomplished; light Three evidence.
claims.alternative: Told as a joke; it shows a mood fix more than a sustained motive.

claims.claim: In a Vevo DSCVR interview quoted by Hey Alma, she said that for the past year she had felt who she was was not enough, kept trying to be cooler, and went back to why she started music.
claims.passage: "A challenge, I think, for the last year," she said in a Vevo DSCVR interview quoted by [Hey Alma](https://www.heyalma.com/?p=51390) in August 2026, was that "I didn't think who I was, you know, what my identity was, was enough. So I kept trying to be cooler than I was. Like, a north-west London Jewish girl who sings jazz, you know?" Then she "went back to why I started doing music."
claims.inference: A time-bound phase of adapting her image, resolved by returning to her reasons for music; fits Three (adapting) and Four (return to authenticity).
claims.alternative: Secondhand via Hey Alma; the original video was not opened, and its date is unknown.

claims.claim: She told Audacy in July 2026 that her 2024 single "Back to Blonde" was not an honest song.
claims.passage: She told [Audacy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=veNH3JQNKR8) in July 2026 that her 2024 single "Back to Blonde" was "not an honest song."
claims.inference: The deficiency language ('was enough') and the return to an 'authentic' self are the Four storyline; the episode itself (adopting a cooler, more produced style that peers were doing) is what a Three does. The correction, not the adaptation, is what she treats as her real self.
claims.alternative: Commercially, the jazz-and-soul turn is what worked ('Die on This Hill'); a Three who followed results would tell the same story. The Vevo quotation is secondhand via Hey Alma.

claims.claim: Her '60s look replaced baggy clothes she wore because she hated being seen; she says her hair felt like armour and made her feel more herself though it looked less like her.
claims.passage: Her '60s look replaced baggy clothes she wore, she told Rolling Stone UK, because she hated the idea of being looked at. "My hair felt like armour. It made me feel more myself, even though it looked less like me."
claims.inference: Identity constructed through aesthetic: a look that felt more like herself; usable for Four (a self she had to build) and Three (an image).
claims.alternative: She also says the uniform "made me feel really secure", which a Six reading could use; body image is a circumstance, not a motive.

claims.claim: Her full-take vocal method began, she told the AP, from being a bit lazy; she now credits the full-take, tape-recorded jazz and soul records she grew up on.
claims.passage: She records whole vocal takes rather than stitching lines together, and she told the AP that "originally it came from me being a bit lazy to be honest." Now she credits the '60s and '70s records she grew up on, cut to tape in full takes.
claims.inference: A candid detail that cuts against a purely romantic authenticity story; it shows she is willing to deflate her own myth in interviews.
claims.alternative: The method is still presented as artistic principle elsewhere (S03, S01); both can be true.

claims.claim: Every first-person source dates from March 2025 to October 2026, nearly all from EP and album promotion.
claims.passage: Every first-person source here dates from March 2025 to October 2026, nearly all of it from promoting an EP and an album.
claims.inference: Dates of the earliest (Principle, 2025-03-10) and latest (Billboard News, 2026-10-02) first-person sources.
claims.alternative: New interviews will extend this range.
claims.review_trigger: At the next refresh, update the date range of first-person sources.

claims.claim: Her manager Miriam Maslin, who has managed her since she was 16, told Music Week the campaign focused on building a world that feels honest and long-term.
claims.passage: Her manager, Miriam Maslin, who had managed her since she was 16, told [Music Week](https://www.musicweek.com/management/read/the-biggest-hope-is-longevity-manager-miriam-maslin-on-sienna-spiro-s-visitor-campaign/094416) in July 2026 that they had "focused on building a world that feels honest and long-term rather than chasing quick moments."
claims.inference: The only sustained named testimony. It confirms a close, trusting relationship (which Spiro calls 'my teammate and my equal') and shows that the authenticity she voices is also an explicit strategy.
claims.alternative: Maslin is an interested party speaking on release day; her account is about the career, not Spiro's inner life.
claims.review_trigger: If Spiro changes management or Maslin speaks again about her, update this claim.

claims.claim: Interpretation: melancholy and candor are her genre's currency, which weakens them as evidence of motive.
claims.passage: Melancholy and candor are her genre's currency. That doesn't make hers false. It makes them weak evidence of motive.
claims.inference: Follows from C28 and the "sad girl singer" framing of her coverage (Interview magazine headline).
claims.alternative: Incentives can coincide with real temperament.

claims.claim: Rolling Stone UK reported her ADHD diagnosis, and she tied it to the visitor feeling: struggling to keep up with people, losing people, being temporary.
claims.passage: Rolling Stone UK reported her ADHD diagnosis, and she tied it to "The Visitor": "struggling to keep up with people and being [too] aware of everything, you end up losing people – and you're temporary."
claims.inference: Her own non-type explanation of the visitor feeling; it is reported, not used as type evidence.
claims.alternative: The writer frames the diagnosis; the quotation is hers.

claims.claim: She told Notion that, neurodivergent and undiagnosed as a child, she kept hearing that she was dramatic, emotional and sad.
claims.passage: Undiagnosed as a child, she told Notion, she kept hearing, "You're so dramatic, you're so emotional, you're so sad!"
claims.inference: A second non-type explanation she offers for her childhood feelings.
claims.alternative: Self-report about childhood; no third-party account.

claims.claim: The article does not infer type from health or health from type.
claims.passage: Nothing here reads a type from her health, or her health from a type.
claims.inference: An explicit limit on inference.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Moment (September 2, 2026) wrote that she and other new stars were given the nepotism-baby and industry-plant labels, which it defined as implying success purchased through connections or money.
claims.passage: In September 2026, [Moment](https://momentmag.com/jewish-nepo-baby-olympics/) wrote that she and other new stars had been given "the typical asterisks that come with sudden fame—nepotism baby, industry plant," labels implying success "purchased" through connections or money.
claims.inference: Relevant as a public framing the article must handle fairly and as the counter-case to her self-presentation of hard-won authenticity. It is not evidence about her motivation.
claims.alternative: Her privilege is real (C02); her own account credits a TikTok-discovered manager and a publishing deal after her breakthrough. Attribute each label to who used it; do not adopt 'industry plant' in the article's voice.
claims.review_trigger: If Spiro addresses the nepotism or industry-plant framing, or if new reporting documents family financing or connections behind her career, update this claim and add her response.

claims.claim: The Moment writer, comparing her with Amy Winehouse in a passage that called Visitor a solid debut, wrote that she seems to emulate emotional turbulence without having experienced it.
claims.passage: Comparing her with Amy Winehouse, in a passage that also called _Visitor_ "a solid debut," the same critic added, "it feels like Spiro emulates the emotional turbulence without having experienced it herself."
claims.inference: One critic's impression, set in its comparative and mixed-to-positive context.
claims.alternative: Her disclosed experiences (bullying she says no one believed, depression in 2025) bear on "without having experienced it".
claims.review_trigger: If she or other critics answer the "emulates" remark, or if Moment revises it, update this claim.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Moment remark is the sharpest form of the counter-case that her sadness is style, and her disclosed experiences bear on it.
claims.passage: That impression is the sharpest form of the counter-case that her sadness is style; the bullying and depression she has described bear on it.
claims.inference: Attributes the counter-case to one critic's remark rather than to the nepotism labels.
claims.alternative: Her disclosures are self-report and do not settle whether her songs reflect them.

claims.claim: The Austin American-Statesman used the nepo-baby label playfully in a rave of her October 9, 2026 Austin City Limits set, finding her heart on her sleeve.
claims.passage: The [Austin American-Statesman](https://www.statesman.com/entertainment/music/article/sienna-spiro-acl-fest-review-22470856.php) used the label playfully, headlining a rave of her October 9, 2026 Austin City Limits set "one of ACL Fest's all-time best nepo baby sets" and finding her "heart is on her sleeve."
claims.inference: A positive eyewitness review that treats her songwriting as heartfelt; it is not a detractor and offers no evidence that family money bought her career.
claims.alternative: The headline uses the label for attention; the body is a rave.

claims.claim: Neither piece shows money or connections bought her career, and no response from her has been found.
claims.passage: Neither piece shows that money or connections bought her career, and as of October 14, 2026, no response from her has been found.
claims.inference: Both pieces were read in full; neither reports evidence of financing. No statement from her was found in the opened sources.
claims.alternative: Her privilege is real; absence of a response may simply mean no one has asked.
claims.review_trigger: If she addresses the nepotism or industry-plant framing, or new reporting documents family financing or connections behind her career, update this sentence and the parents FAQ.

claims.claim: She told Interview that she found her management from posting one video.
claims.passage: Her own account of her start is TikTok: she found her management, she told Interview, "from posting one video."
claims.inference: Her own on-record account of how she was found, set beside the nepotism framing.
claims.alternative: Self-report; family connections could also have helped in ways not on record.

claims.claim: Metadata: nepotism framing and absence of evidence or response, dated.

No reporting found by October 14, 2026 shows that family money or connections bought her career, and no public response from her was found.
claims.inference: Same as C64, dated for the FAQ.
claims.alternative: As C64.
claims.review_trigger: Same trigger as C64.

claims.claim: Metadata: she has said she found her manager by posting a video.
claims.passage: She has said she found her manager by posting a video.
claims.inference: Parents FAQ: her own account of her start.
claims.alternative: Self-report.

claims.claim: As of October 14, 2026, the people who had described her on record were her manager, critics and her grandmother Sheila, who said on a Capital segment in April 2026 that she was not a nightmare but had her own opinion on most things.
claims.passage: As of that date, the people who had described her on record were her manager, critics who saw single shows, and her grandmother, Sheila, who told a Capital segment in April 2026 that Sienna was "not a nightmare, but she had her own personal opinion on most things."
claims.inference: The only family testimony in the record; it is light and affectionate and fits her self-description as headstrong.
claims.alternative: No speaker labels; the attribution follows the host's question to "Grandma Sheila". A playful on-air remark.
claims.review_trigger: When testimony from a sibling, classmate or long-time collaborator appears, revise this sentence.

claims.claim: No sibling, school friend or longtime collaborator has spoken about her.
claims.passage: No sibling, school friend or longtime collaborator had spoken.
claims.inference: Across 41 logged sources, the only testimony is her manager, critics and her grandmother.
claims.alternative: Absence in the record, not proof of absence.
claims.review_trigger: When testimony from a sibling, classmate or long-time collaborator (e.g. Omer Fedi) appears, add it and revise.

claims.claim: Type 2 case: her most explicit self-description, repeated in at least five interviews from November 2025 to June 2026, is that she made herself needed because people would not want her otherwise; in 2026 she still described conditional belonging and giving.
claims.passage: The Two case rests on her most explicit self-description, returned to in at least five interviews between November 2025 and June 2026: she made herself needed because she didn't think people would want her otherwise. It is not only history. In 2026 she still defined the visitor feeling as being "expired" unless she keeps showing up, and said she gives "a lot of myself."
claims.inference: SSENSE (November 2025), Genius (February 2026), Z100 (March 2026), Capital (April 2026) and Zach Sang (June 2026) each describe earning a place by giving, showing up or mirroring; the core belief ("never thought people would want me otherwise if they didn't need me") is the Two's, stated in her words.
claims.alternative: A learned response to weight-based exclusion in childhood could produce the same strategy in another type; all five are promotional interviews.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess at the 2026-12-01 review, after the February 7, 2027 Grammy ceremony, or when any settle signal in open_case.settle_signals appears.

claims.claim: Type 2 strain: when the person she wants is out of reach, she describes waiting, imagining and writing, not giving more, and says it has happened many times.
claims.passage: What strains it is where giving isn't possible. When the person she wants is out of reach, she doesn't describe doing more for them. She waits, imagines them into the doorway and writes the song, and says it has happened "so many different times."
claims.inference: The New York man (2025), "You Stole the Show" (2025) and "so many different times" (August 2026) show a repeated longing response the Two reading predicts less well.
claims.alternative: Twos also pine for unavailable people; with no way to give, waiting may be the only option open to any type.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess at the 2026-12-01 review, after the February 7, 2027 Grammy ceremony, or when any settle signal in open_case.settle_signals appears.

claims.claim: Type 4 case: the longing pattern, sadness as temperament, envy of her own imagination, feeling unreal except when singing, and a look that made her feel more herself.
claims.passage: The Four case rests on that longing and on what singing gives her. She calls sadness her temperament, envies her own imagination and sometimes doesn't feel like a real person except when she sings, a concern the Two reading predicts less well. Even the '60s hair she calls armour made her feel "more myself, even though it looked less like me."
claims.inference: Identity and reality concerns ("I just don't feel like a real person", October 2026; singing as "the way I felt like a real person", June 2026) are closer to the Four's core fear than to the Two's.
claims.alternative: Numbness and unreality also follow from the depression and ADHD she has disclosed; melancholy is her genre's currency.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess at the 2026-12-01 review, after the February 7, 2027 Grammy ceremony, or when any settle signal in open_case.settle_signals appears.

claims.claim: Type 4 strain: she describes her feelings as shared, not as setting her apart; the unreality has health confounds; most definitions of the visitor feeling concern conditional belonging.
claims.passage: Against it, she describes her feelings as shared, not as what sets her apart. Sadness is "a very normal, human way to be," and asked by [Euphoria](https://www.euphoriazine.com/blog/2026/08/interviews-sienna-spiro/) in August 2026 whether she sees herself as a visitor in life generally, she said, "We all are visitors in a way, aren't we?" The unreality comes with numbness and depression she has disclosed, and most of her definitions of the visitor feeling are about being kept while useful.
claims.inference: The Four's marker of feeling fundamentally apart is missing from her self-description (Vogue, July 2026; Euphoria, August 2026).
claims.alternative: Promotional interviews reward relatability, so "shared" framing may be format.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess at the 2026-12-01 review, after the February 7, 2027 Grammy ceremony, or when any settle signal in open_case.settle_signals appears.

claims.claim: Type 3 case and counter: drive, the cooler phase, a disowned single and an image-conscious look; against it, volunteered sadness and rejecting applause, though on a night it did not come.
claims.passage: The Three case is the drive, from the school campaign to the suit, plus the cooler phase, a single she now calls dishonest, and a look that is also an image. Against it, she volunteers sadness and wrote off applause as "other people's agenda" on a night it didn't come, which could be a save as easily as a principle.
claims.inference: Three remains live on behavior; the counter-evidence is costless and ambiguous.
claims.alternative: Drive is common to ambitious people of any type.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess at the 2026-12-01 review, after the February 7, 2027 Grammy ceremony, or when any settle signal in open_case.settle_signals appears.

claims.claim: Type 3 case and its limit.
claims.passage: Those choices have cost her nothing measurable, though, and they fit the brand her manager describes.
claims.inference: Why Three stays live: her authenticity choices are not yet costly.
claims.alternative: A later costly choice for or against reach would discriminate.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess when she explains her second album.

claims.claim: Interpretation: Three ranks third because the fear she names is being unwanted, not failing.
claims.passage: Three ranks third because what she says she fears is being unwanted, not failing.
claims.inference: Her named fear (Z100, March 2026) is relational; she told NYLON that fixating on numbers and people liking her would make her miserable.
claims.alternative: Self-report of fears can understate achievement anxiety.
claims.review_trigger: Re-assess at the 2026-12-01 review, after the February 7, 2027 Grammy ceremony, or when any settle signal in open_case.settle_signals appears.

claims.claim: Type 6 set aside: Variety heard deeply held anxieties and she calls herself an over-thinker and a control freak, but the fears she names are shame-family (rejection, embarrassment, being temporary) rather than safety and support.
claims.passage: The Six case is real: Willman heard a writer "motivated to write songs by some deeply held anxieties," and she calls herself "quite an over-thinker" and "a control freak." But the fears she names (rejection, embarrassment, being temporary to people) are the heart triad's shame more than the Six's fear for safety and support.
claims.inference: Names the strongest Six evidence and sets it aside on the emotion she names (embarrassment, rejection), not on the producer's promise.
claims.alternative: She says her '60s uniform "made me feel really secure" and has trusted one manager since 16; a Six reading could use both.

claims.claim: Type 9 set aside: she mirrors people to be kept around, which points to attachment and approval rather than merging for peace, and she rarely mutes her opinions.
claims.passage: Her numbness and mirroring suggest Nine, but she mirrors people, she said, "to be kept around," the Two's bargain rather than a Nine's merging for peace, and she rarely mutes her opinions.
claims.inference: The stated purpose of the mirroring (Genius, February 2026) discriminates; her grandmother and Vogue describe a strongly opinionated person.
claims.alternative: She defers to trusted collaborators (Omer Fedi), which a Nine reading could use.

claims.claim: Verdict: Two leads on the pattern she calls the theme of her life and still describes in 2026; Four is close on longing and unreality; both come from album promotion.
claims.passage: Two leads because the pattern she calls the theme of her whole life, making herself needed so people will keep her, is the Two's, and she still described it that way in 2026. Four is close because the pattern that appears wherever she can't give, longing for someone absent and feeling unreal except when she sings, is the Four's. Both come from interviews promoting an album about exactly these feelings, so neither can carry the weight yet.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The longing pattern, repeated across 2025-26: when the person she wants is out of reach she waits, imagines them present and writes the song (the New York man, C21, C79; 'You Stole the Show', C94, C45; 'so many different times', C44), not the Two's move of giving more (C115). (2) Identity and reality concerns closer to the Four's core fear: singing as 'the way I felt like a real person' and 'I just don't feel like a real person' (C40, C47), and a look that made her feel 'more myself' (C100). (3) She presents sadness as temperament (C06) and leads with her own feelings, though that is partly the format of promotional interviews about confessional songs. (4) Confounds on the Two side: the helper strategy began as a response to weight-based exclusion in childhood (C48), a circumstance that could teach any type to make itself useful; every statement is from album or EP promotion (C59, C60). (5) Drive and image work keep Three live (C03, C17, C38, C14, C57).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4 is the closest rival. It rests on the longing pattern (C21, C44, C94, C45, C115), sadness as temperament (C06), unreality except when singing (C40, C47) and an aesthetic self she had to construct (C100) (C83). What strains it: she describes her feelings as shared, not as setting her apart ('a very normal, human way to be', C93; 'We all are visitors in a way, aren't we?', C111); the unreality comes with disclosed numbness, depression and ADHD (C26, C62); and most of her definitions of the visitor feeling are about being kept while useful (C96, C22, C09). Type 3 is also live: the ELAM campaign, over-singing for validation, the suit, the 'cooler' phase and a single she calls dishonest (C03, C57, C17, C38, C14); against it, she volunteers sadness and rejected applause on a night it did not come, both costless (C112, C85); her named fear is being unwanted, not failing (C116). Types 6 and 9 were tested and set aside. Six: Variety's 'deeply held anxieties', over-thinking and control (C33), but the fears she names are rejection, embarrassment and being temporary, shame rather than safety (C110, C39). Nine: numbness and mirroring, but she mirrors 'to be kept around' and is strongly opinionated (C105).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: None that is defensible yet. Two versus Four turns on what she does when someone she cares about pulls back. In friendships she describes the Two move in the present tense: initiating, showing up, giving more than she gets and feeling taken advantage of (C96, C52, C114). With unavailable romantic interests she describes the Four move: waiting, idealizing and turning the absence into a song (C21, C44, C94). The draft's tense test (helping past, withdrawal present) was wrong: the closed-off withdrawal is told as a past phase she rejected (C10, C97), 'if you don't want me, don't have me' is acceptance of endings followed by a case for her value (C54, C98), and the giving is present tense (C52). All of it is self-narrated in promotion for an album about exactly these feelings. A friend's or sibling's account of her in a cooling friendship would separate the readings. For Four versus Three, the discriminator is a choice where her own feeling costs her reach or approval; the examples so far (disowning 'Back to Blonde', rejecting applause) cost her nothing measurable (C85).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her drive and competitiveness (C03, C55, C17) are not well explained by Two or Four. Her accounts of the 'Die on This Hill' arrangement differ about who was right (Vogue says producer Omer Fedi was correct; NYLON has her overruling someone who liked an acoustic version), so the edit no longer prints either as a pattern. She says both that saying things aloud jinxes them and that she manifests things. Her full-take method began as laziness and became principle (C20). The cheerful, joking register of her interviews fits the Two reading better than her self-description as naturally sad and numb (C06, C40).

open_case.reason: Sienna Spiro turned 21 on September 28, 2026. She has posted singing videos on TikTok since 2021 and released her first single in May 2024, but her breakthrough, 'Die on This Hill', came on October 10, 2025, and her debut album on July 3, 2026. Every first-person interview opened (about 30, March 2025 to October 2026) belongs to the EP and album promotion cycles, in which the same stories recur and confessional authenticity is both her genre's currency and her manager's stated strategy. The only named testimony comes from her manager (an interested party), her grandmother in a radio segment, and critics who saw single shows. No sibling, school friend, classmate or long-time collaborator has spoken about her. Forty-one sources were logged (39 opened), and Types 2, 3, 4, 6 and 9 were tested. The leading read (Two) and the strongest alternative (Four) both have direct, repeated first-person support; the behavior that would separate them, how she acts when a friendship cools, described by someone other than her, is not yet on record.
settle_signals: A friendship that cools after her fame. She already says she gives more than she gets (June and April 2026). Does she keep initiating, being the 'therapist' friend and feeling used when it is not returned (Two), or pull back, grieve privately and write about being temporary (Four)? An account from the friend would count for more than hers.

Her second album. A brighter record she explains as what audiences wanted favors Three; one she calls truer to herself at a cost in reach favors Four; one built around a costly choice for one person, such as handing a collaborator the spotlight, favors Two. Hoping the songs help listeners does not count; she already says that.

A major award result, starting with the 2027 Grammys (nominations November 16, 2026; ceremony February 7, 2027). Win or snub, does she treat it as proof and name the next target (Three), say it does not feel real or that she has been misread (Four), or talk about who wants her around (Two)? Thanking her team does not count.

The first on-record account from someone who knew her before 2022 (a sister, an ELAM classmate, a teacher or an early collaborator) describing her in a group: the friend who looks after everyone and makes the plans (Two), the intense one who feels apart (Four), or the driven one working the room (Three).

A cost she pays for a feeling, such as keeping a sad set when a festival crowd wants the hits or turning down a lucrative feature that is not her: paying it favors Four; dropping it when the numbers dip favors Three; paying it to protect a friend or collaborator favors Two.
